Read Today's Paper Muthoot Finance Q2 cons profit jumps 36% YoY to Rs 3,278 crore SECTIONS Muthoot Finance Q2 cons profit jumps 36% YoY to Rs 3,278 crore By Atmadip Ray , ET Bureau Last Updated: Oct 31, 2026, 06:15:00 PM IST Rate Story Follow us Share Font Size Abc Small Abc Medium Abc Large Save Print Comment Synopsis Muthoot Finance reported a 36% year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 3,278 crore in Q2, while assets under management grew 42% to Rs 2.09 lakh crore. However, standalone gross NPA ratio rose to 3.87% from 2.28% in the previous quarter, indicating a deterioration in asset quality Reuters For 9 months, profit after tax surged 91% year-on-year to Rs 7,048 crore, compared with Rs 3,693 crore in the corresponding period last year. Kolkata: India's largest gold loan company Muthoot Finance reported a 36% year-on-year surge in consolidated net profit for the second quarter at Rs 3,278 crore, backed by 42% expansion in business while asset quality deteriorated. The net profit was Rs 2,412 crore in the year ago period. On a standalone basis, the company's second quarter net profit stood at Rs 2977 crore, up 27% over Rs 2345 in the year-ago quarter. Muthoot's consolidated assets under management grew 42% year-on-year to Rs 2.09 lakh crore at the end of September. Out of this, the gold loan stood at Rs 1.93 lakh crore. Its standalone AUM grew at the same pace to Rs 1.88 lakh crore, of which gold loan was Rs 1.79 lakh crore. Live Events The company's standalone gross non-performing assets ratio jumped to 3.87% at the end of September from 2.28% three months prior. Muthoot's subsidiary Belstar Microfinance earned a Rs 78 crore net profit for the quarter under review, widening from Rs 66 crore in the first quarter. Its asset quality improved with gross NPA ratio falling to 3.26% from 4.58% a year back. Its first half net profit stood at Rs 144 crore compared to a loss of Rs 160 crore in the year-ago six month. Its AUM stood at Rs 7,876 crore at the end of September against Rs 7,715 crore a year prior as industry-wide stress moderated disbursement growth, the company said. He expects the index to target 35,000 as global profit-booking in AI and semiconductor stocks drives capital rotation towards Indian IT. This was also supported by the global rotation away from AI and semiconductor stocks amid profit booking. There will be no fresh mainboard IPO launches, although several companies that raised funds in late October are preparing for their stock market debuts. Vedant Poly Fabs, a small and medium enterprise (SME), will be the only new company opening its IPO next week. Meanwhile, six companies whose public issues are currently open, including mainboard player Bombay Coated & Special Steels, are scheduled to list on the exchanges during the week. The slowdown follows a busy October for India's primary market, highlighted by Jio Platforms ' Rs 30,188 crore IPO, the largest in the country's history. Mukesh Ambani-led Jio made its stock market debut on October 28 at Rs 1,358, a premium of 21.36% over its issue price of Rs 1,119. The blockbuster offering attracted bids worth Rs 4.9 lakh crore in the public book and was subscribed more than 22 times. The coming week will see investors turn their attention towards the final subscription days of existing issues and the listing performance of recently concluded offerings. Live Events Vedant Poly Fabs IPOThe Rs 56.68 crore IPO of Vedant Poly Fabs will open for public subscription on Monday, November 2, and close on Wednesday, November 4. The company has fixed a price band of Rs 88-94 per share. The offering comprises a fresh issue of 54.26 lakh shares worth Rs 51.01 crore and an offer for sale of 6.04 lakh shares aggregating to Rs 5.67 crore. Retail investors will have to apply for a minimum of 2,400 shares, requiring an investment of Rs 2,25,600 at the upper end of the price band. The company is expected to finalise the basis of allotment on November 5, with its tentative listing on the NSE SME platform scheduled for November 9. The regulatory body discovered that the company recognized revenue too early and inflated expenses, distorting profit reports. In addition to the company's penalties totaling Rs 88 lakh, several executives were also fined for their complicity in these discrepancies. Agencies Markets regulator Sebi has barred EKI Energy Services Ltd and its Managing Director Manish Kumar Dabkara from the securities market for two months and 12 months, respectively, for misrepresenting financial statements of the carbon credits trading firm and diverting funds. Also, the regulator has restrained the company's former Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Mohit Kumar Agarwal from the securities market for eight months, while whole-time directors Naveen Sharma and Sonali Sheikh have been prohibited for five months and one month, respectively. Besides, Sebi has imposed monetary penalties totalling Rs 88 lakh on the company and other individuals for various violations of securities market regulations. Further, the markets regulator directed Dabkara to take immediate steps to recoup the amount diverted from EKI Energy Services. In its 94-page final order, Sebi noted that EKI had prematurely recognised revenue aggregating Rs 197.04 crore during the first three quarters of FY23, thereby misrepresenting its financial performance to investors. Live Events The regulator observed that "EKI's publication and continued disclosure of prematurely recognised revenue of Rs 197.04 crore constituted reckless financial misrepresentation connected with investor decisions concerning its listed shares". Also, the regulator found that EKI had overstated expenses by Rs 26.34 crore during FY22 and FY23, resulting in an understatement of its profits. "The company diverted Rs 26.34 crore by overstating expenses during 2021-22 and 2022-23," the order said. The regulator noted that EKI had "booked fictitious expenses against services not rendered", adding that payments made against such expenses "consequently constituted diversion of EKI's funds". Also, Sebi noted that Dabkara was responsible for the continued disclosure of misstated financial information and failure to ensure proper monitoring of the company's financial reporting systems. Also, the regulator held Sharma, Sheikh, and Agarwal liable for regulatory violations. Sebi imposed a penalty of Rs 12 lakh on EKI Energy Services, Rs 28 lakh on Dabkara, Rs 13 lakh on Sharma, Rs 6 lakh on Sheikh and Rs 19 lakh on Agarwal. Sebi also imposed monetary penalties on independent directors Ritesh Gupta and Burhanuddin Ali Husain Maksi Wala, besides former compliance officer Itisha Sahu. ET CONTRIBUTORS Imagine building a business, attracting investors, creating thousands of jobs and investing billions in infrastructure, only to discover that a regulatory change has fundamentally rewritten the economics of your business overnight. Your customers haven't changed, and your operations remain the same, but the rules of the game have. This is where the relationship between regulation and free markets becomes complicated. Free markets thrive on competition, innovation and commercial freedom. Regulation, on the other hand, is essential to protect consumers, prevent the misuse of market power and build trust. The challenge begins when intervention goes beyond correcting market failures and starts altering the economic incentives that make businesses viable. For investors, regulation is not merely a compliance matter; it can fundamentally change the earnings potential, valuation and long-term attractiveness of an entire industry. Also Read | ET Wealth Expo: Why market veteran S Naren thinks investors are getting gold, silver and asset allocation all wrong India's insurance sector offers a recent illustration. In September, insurance stocks came under pressure following proposed regulatory changes by IRDAI concerning commissions and distribution practices. The intention is understandable: curb mis-selling, improve transparency, reduce distribution costs and ultimately deliver better value to policyholders. However, for insurers and intermediaries, distribution economics are central to profitability. A sudden change in these economics can affect earnings visibility, business expansion and investor sentiment. What the regulator sees as consumer protection , the market initially interprets as an earnings risk. Agencies Both perspectives can be valid. Live Events Not all regulation, however, creates a conflict between business interests and consumer welfare. The government's decision to cap trade margins on non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines is an example of intervention aimed at improving affordability and access to essential treatment. Similarly, the RBI's regulatory framework for the UPI ecosystem has helped create trust, interoperability and scale in India's digital payments revolution. In both cases, regulation has played an enabling role by addressing market frictions and improving consumer outcomes. The problem arises when the immediate objective of intervention overshadows its longer-term economic consequences. Consider India's agricultural export restrictions. Measures such as export bans and duties have often been introduced to protect domestic availability and contain food inflation. Agencies Three leading global beverage companies - Carlsberg, Pernod Ricard and The Coca-Cola Company - are advancing their plans for potential listings of their Indian businesses, albeit at different stages, as they prepare to tap the domestic capital market and join the growing pipeline of large offerings. In their latest earnings calls, top executives from the three companies outlined progress on their respective listing plans, with Carlsberg filing an updated draft red herring prospectus, Pernod Ricard continuing preparatory work pending board approval, and Coca-Cola exploring a potential IPO of its Indian bottling operations. The developments underline the growing interest among multinational beverage companies in unlocking value from their Indian operations through public listings, although the proposed offerings remain subject to varying regulatory, corporate and market-related considerations. Among them, Danish brewer Carlsberg is the furthest along, having filed an updated draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). Carlsberg Chief Financial Officer Ulrica Fearn, during the company's latest earnings call for the third quarter of 2026, confirmed that an updated DRHP was filed with SEBI on October 28, which is available on the regulator's website and Carlsberg's India website. Live Events Though she declined to "comment further on the outcome or timing on such a potential IPO" due to regulatory requirements, she said follow-on activities customary in such a process, including arranging interactions with potential investors, indicating that preparations are progressing beyond the initial documentation stage. "As it is customary in such a process, we are now engaging follow-on activities, including setting up interactions with potential investors," Fearn said. Replying to a query on the India IPO , Carlsberg Chief Executive Officer, Jacob Aarup-Andersen, said: "... the IPO is progressing. Ulrika Fearn also mentioned that we are now calling meetings with potential investors." He also refrained from providing further details on the potential offering, including its timeline and outcome. Andersen also declined to comment specifically on the performance of its Indian business or make comparisons with competitors, citing regulatory restrictions linked to the prospective IPO.
